anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve is injured by a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus, and what is the classic mechanism?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The axillary nerve (C5–C6). Also injured by anterior shoulder dislocation.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What motor and sensory deficit results from an axillary nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Motor: deltoid (abduction 15–90°) and teres minor. Sensory: the “regimental badge” area over the lateral shoulder.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove and is injured by a midshaft humeral fracture?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The radial nerve — producing wrist drop. Also compressed in “Saturday night palsy”.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the motor and sensory loss with a radial nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Motor: wrist & finger extensors, supinator, triceps → wrist drop. Sensory: dorsal 1st web space.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Where are the two classic sites of median nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The carpal tunnel (wrist) and a supracondylar fracture (elbow).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What muscles does the median nerve supply in the hand (mnemonic)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: LOAF: Lateral 2 lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis (plus most forearm flexors).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the sensory territory of the median nerve in the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The lateral (radial) 3½ fingers on the palmar side.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Where are the two classic sites of ulnar nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Behind the medial epicondyle / cubital tunnel (elbow) and Guyon’s canal (wrist, between pisiform & hook of hamate).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What does the ulnar nerve supply in the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The intrinsic muscles: interossei, hypothenar muscles, medial 2 lumbricals and adductor pollicis. Sensory: medial 1½ fingers.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve supplies serratus anterior and what deformity follows its injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) → winged scapula. Classic cause: axillary node clearance / mastectomy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the “hand of benediction” — which nerve and when is it seen?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A median nerve lesion: on trying to make a fist the index & middle fingers can’t flex and stay pointing (a high lesion).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the “ape hand” deformity?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A median nerve sign at rest: thenar wasting with the thumb pulled into the plane of the palm (lost opposition & abduction).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Describe the ulnar claw hand.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Ring & little fingers hyperextended at the MCP joints and flexed at the IP joints — loss of the medial 2 lumbricals/interossei with unopposed long flexors/extensors.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the ulnar paradox?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A higher (elbow) ulnar lesion produces a less obvious claw, because the medial half of FDP is also paralysed so the fingertips can’t curl. The claw worsens with a distal lesion or as a proximal one recovers.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is Froment’s sign and what does it test?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: To hold paper between thumb & index the patient flexes FPL (median) to compensate for a weak adductor pollicis (ulnar) — a sign of ulnar nerve palsy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the roots, mechanism and posture of Erb’s palsy?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: C5–C6 (upper trunk). Excess head–shoulder separation (shoulder dystocia / fall on shoulder). Posture: adducted, internally rotated, extended elbow, pronated forearm = “waiter’s tip”.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the roots and features of Klumpke’s palsy?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: C8–T1 (lower trunk). Loss of the hand intrinsics → claw hand; may injure T1 sympathetics → Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Give the order of the brachial plexus from proximal to distal.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches (“Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”). Roots C5–T1; cords named by their relation to the axillary artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: A midshaft clavicle fracture: what is the commonest site and what pulls the medial fragment up?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The middle third is commonest; the medial fragment is elevated by sternocleidomastoid.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Why does a proximal-pole scaphoid fracture risk avascular necrosis and non-union?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Its blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde, so a proximal fracture starves the proximal fragment.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: How should you manage a FOOSH with anatomical snuffbox tenderness but a normal X-ray?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Treat as a scaphoid fracture: immobilise in a thumb spica and re-image (repeat X-ray or MRI) in 10–14 days — never discharge as a sprain.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the borders and floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Borders: EPL (ulnar side); APL + EPB (radial side). Floor: scaphoid & trapezium. The radial artery crosses it.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Distinguish a Colles’ from a Smith’s fracture.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Colles’ = distal radius with dorsal angulation (“dinner-fork”), FOOSH in the elderly. Smith’s = volar angulation (“reverse Colles’”), fall on a flexed wrist.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What passes through the carpal tunnel?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: 9 flexor tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) plus the median nerve, deep to the flexor retinaculum.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Why is thenar skin sensation spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the tunnel and runs superficial to the retinaculum, so it is not compressed (though the thenar muscles waste).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Name two bedside tests for carpal tunnel syndrome.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Tinel’s sign (tapping over the nerve) and Phalen’s test (sustained wrist flexion) reproduce the paraesthesia.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the four rotator cuff muscles and which is most commonly torn?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: SITS: Supraspinatus (initiates abduction 0–15°, most commonly torn), Infraspinatus & teres minor (external rotation), Subscapularis (internal rotation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the commonest direction of shoulder dislocation and which nerve must you check?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Anterior (~95%). Document axillary nerve function (regimental-badge sensation & deltoid) before and after reduction.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the contents of the cubital fossa (lateral → medial)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: TAN: biceps Tendon · brachial Artery · median Nerve. The median cubital vein crosses the roof (venepuncture site).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the “6 Ps” of compartment syndrome and the key management point?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Pain (out of proportion & on passive stretch — earliest), Paraesthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness (late), Paralysis, Perishingly cold. Treat with emergency fasciotomy — don’t wait for a lost pulse.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture and its classic cause?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A fixed flexion contracture of the wrist & fingers from untreated forearm compartment syndrome — classically after a supracondylar fracture injuring the brachial artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: How are axillary lymph nodes grouped, and what do they drain?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Levels I–III relative to pectoralis minor (I below, II behind, III above). They drain the upper limb and ~75% of the breast — key in breast cancer staging.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A 30-year-old sustains a spiral fracture of the mid-shaft of the humerus. On examination he cannot extend his wrist or fingers, but elbow flexion and shoulder movement are intact. Which nerve is injured?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humeral shaft; a mid-shaft fracture injures it, paralysing the wrist and finger extensors → wrist drop. Triceps (a higher branch) is often spared.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient dislocates their shoulder anteriorly. Which single examination finding most specifically indicates the associated nerve injury?
options: Loss of sensation over the medial forearm
Loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder (‘regimental badge’)
Clawing of the ring and little fingers
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Anterior shoulder dislocation (and surgical-neck fractures) endanger the axillary nerve. It supplies sensation to the ‘regimental badge’ area over the deltoid and motor supply to deltoid/teres minor.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A child falls onto an outstretched hand and sustains a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. Which structures are most at risk, and what is the feared late complication?
options: Ulnar nerve and ulnar artery; Dupuytren’s contracture
Median nerve and brachial artery; Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture
Radial nerve and cephalic vein; wrist drop
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex artery; deltoid wasting
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A supracondylar fracture threatens the median nerve (especially the anterior interosseous branch) and the brachial artery. Arterial injury → forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A young adult has persistent wrist pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall. The initial X-ray is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure and discharge as a wrist sprain
Immobilise in a thumb spica and re-image in 10–14 days
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Prescribe analgesia and arrange routine physiotherapy
Apply a below-elbow cast for 48 hours only
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise, and scaphoid fractures are often occult on the first film. Immobilise and re-image (repeat X-ray/MRI) — missing it risks avascular necrosis and non-union.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Why is a proximal-pole scaphoid fracture particularly prone to avascular necrosis?
options: The scaphoid has no blood supply at all
Its blood supply enters proximally and flows distally
Its blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a proximal fracture cuts it off
It is bathed in synovial fluid which prevents healing
The radial artery is always torn in the injury
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The scaphoid’s blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde. A proximal-pole fracture therefore starves the proximal fragment, causing avascular necrosis and non-union.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: On being asked to make a fist, a patient’s index and middle fingers remain extended while the ring and little fingers curl normally. Which lesion does this indicate?
options: A low ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist
A high median nerve lesion (‘hand of benediction’)
A radial nerve lesion in the axilla
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: This is the hand of benediction — a high median nerve lesion. The median-supplied flexors to the index and middle fingers are paralysed, so they cannot flex when making a fist, while the ulnar-supplied ring/little fingers curl normally.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient has an ulnar nerve laceration. Counter-intuitively, which lesion location produces the MORE pronounced claw hand?
options: A lesion at the elbow (higher lesion)
A lesion at the wrist (lower/distal lesion)
A lesion in the brachial plexus
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The ulnar paradox: a distal (wrist) lesion gives a more obvious claw. A higher (elbow) lesion also paralyses the medial half of FDP, so the fingertips cannot flex and the claw is less marked. The claw worsens as a proximal lesion recovers.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A newborn delivered with shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted, internally rotated, with the elbow extended and forearm pronated — the ‘waiter’s tip’ posture. Which roots are affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: This is Erb’s palsy — an upper trunk (C5–C6) injury from excessive head–shoulder separation. Loss of abductors, external rotators and elbow flexors/supinators produces the waiter’s tip posture.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient has weakness of the small muscles of the hand and a claw deformity after a lower brachial plexus (C8–T1) injury. Which additional finding may accompany it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Klumpke’s palsy (C8–T1) can involve the nearby T1 sympathetic fibres, producing an ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) in addition to the claw hand.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient with carpal tunnel syndrome has paraesthesia of the lateral fingers and thenar wasting, but sensation over the thenar eminence skin is preserved. What explains the spared skin sensation?
options: The ulnar nerve supplies the thenar skin
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the tunnel and bypasses it
Sensory fibres regenerate faster than motor fibres
The radial nerve supplies the thenar eminence
The skin is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves the main trunk proximal to the flexor retinaculum and runs superficial to it, so it escapes compression in the tunnel — thenar skin sensation is spared even though the thenar muscles waste.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Froment’s sign is positive when a patient flexes the thumb’s interphalangeal joint to grip a piece of paper. Which muscle is weak, and which nerve is affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Adductor pollicis (ulnar-innervated) is weak, so the patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median) — flexing the thumb IP joint — to hold the paper. A positive Froment’s sign indicates ulnar nerve palsy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates the first 15° of shoulder abduction and is the most commonly torn?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates abduction (0–15°, thereafter deltoid takes over) and is the most commonly torn/impinged cuff muscle. Infraspinatus and teres minor externally rotate; subscapularis internally rotates.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Listing the contents of the cubital fossa from lateral to medial, which sequence is correct?
options: Median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon
Biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Brachial artery, median nerve, biceps tendon
Radial nerve, brachial artery, ulnar nerve
Biceps tendon, median nerve, brachial artery
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Lateral to medial the cubital fossa contains the biceps Tendon, brachial Artery and median Nerve (‘TAN’). The median cubital vein lies in the roof and is the usual venepuncture site.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient with a forearm injury develops severe pain that is worse on passive finger extension, out of proportion to the injury. Distal pulses are still present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Elevate the limb above the heart and observe overnight
Urgent fasciotomy — do not wait for pulselessness
Arrange an outpatient nerve conduction study
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Pain out of proportion and on passive stretch is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome. Pulselessness is a late sign — waiting for it risks irreversible muscle necrosis (Volkmann’s contracture). Emergency fasciotomy is indicated.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A man wakes after falling asleep with his arm draped over the back of a chair and cannot extend his wrist. Which nerve is affected and what is this called?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Prolonged compression of the radial nerve against the humerus (‘Saturday night palsy’) causes wrist drop from paralysis of the wrist/finger extensors, typically with good recovery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: An elderly woman falls onto an outstretched hand and has a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation, giving a ‘dinner-fork’ deformity. What is this fracture called?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A Colles’ fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (‘dinner-fork’ deformity), typically after a FOOSH in the elderly. A Smith’s fracture is the reverse — volar angulation from a fall on a flexed wrist.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Following an axillary lymph node clearance, a patient cannot fully raise the arm above the head and the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall when pushing against a wall. Which nerve was injured?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) supplies serratus anterior and is vulnerable during axillary surgery. Its injury causes a winged scapula and loss of full overhead abduction (impaired scapular rotation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A keen cyclist develops numbness of the little finger and weakness of the hand’s intrinsic muscles after long rides, with sparing of the dorsal ulnar skin. Where is the lesion?
options: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow)
Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Handlebar pressure compresses the ulnar nerve in Guyon’s canal at the wrist (‘cyclist’s palsy’). Because the dorsal cutaneous branch leaves proximal to the canal, sensation over the dorsal ulnar hand is spared — helping localise the lesion to the wrist.
